items.title: Jack Lesberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: I played with Teagarden and Maxie and Peanuts Hucko and Cliff Leeman

ctx.x: Yeah, Ray. I went up to work on 52nd Street and I played with Teagarden and Maxie and Peanuts Hucko and Cliff Leeman, whose wife is here. And Louis came in and sat in and played with us at The Famous Door. That’s where I was working. But 52nd Street was just full of those places you know. Billie Holiday was singing on one corner and you’d just walk down the street or cut over and stand across the street and hear who you wanted to hear from the other place. Yeah it was really a kick, 52nd Street. You’ll never see…
Yeah some of us were born in the wrong era I think.

items.title: 68087_Cliff Leeman oral history interview
items.q: I worked there with Jack Lesberg. He and I -- he was bass drummer and I was the house drummer

ctx.x: years, that I just can't put my finger on many of them without research. Until we came to the point of Dick Gibson, and his World's Greatest Jazz Band, and he opened into the Roosevelt Grill in New York, and had a music policy there. That's another one of his wonderful promotions for jazz music.

I worked there with Jack Lesberg. He and I -- he was bass drummer and I was the house drummer, and we worked there with such groups as Joe Venuti as a leader for awhile, and Buck Clayton a couple of times, and we had Peanuts Hucko for a leader -- we were what you called the intermission band, I guess. While the World's Greatest Jazz Band took time off.

I'll get to the time that I was there with Bobby Hackett because we made five or six albums while playing live from there. One of the greatest albums I ever made in my own personal taste, was the last album. The sound and the soloist and he fours that I took, and so forth, were to me, the best -- the epitome of my playing, if I may say -- for my liking, the band was Dave McKenna on piano, Jack Lesberg on bass, Bobby Hackett and he made it a co-feature with Bobby Hackett, featuring Vic Dickenson.
